source.title: Characterizing Well-behaved vs. Pathological Deep Neural Network Architectures

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents reading.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes random networks at initialization and measures signal/noise moments and sensitivity over depth. These are theoretical and experimental indicators of pathologies related to trainability, but it does not measure training classification error or test whether gradient training reaches zero error.
record.gate_note: The paper's results concern initialization-time propagation and sensitivity, not training outcomes or classification error. Its CIFAR-10 experiments use randomly initialized networks and report moments, effective rank and sensitivity. No training-error rows are warranted. Initialization and architecture findings bear on V4's trainability-related framing, but do not directly measure V4's named training-speed or trainable-depth outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes randomly initialized networks and measures signal/noise moments, effective rank and input sensitivity. It reports no optimization trajectories, training error, training speed or maximum trainable depth. These related initialization measures do not test V1–V6. Section 4 motivates their relevance to optimization using arguments and cited training results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the analyzed initialization setting. The authors attribute feedforward signal and sensitivity pathologies to multiplicative layer composition, and the slower, power-law sensitivity growth of batch-normalized residual networks to dilution of residual branches by skip connections. The residual theorem requires bounded branch signal variances and sensitivity increments; the reported experiments show preserved signal directions and no identified pathology. These conclusions do not demonstrate training performance.
record.recipe_differences: Initialization-time propagation analysis rather than gradient-based training and classification-error measurement; it tracks signal and noise moments, effective rank, and normalized sensitivity.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that batch-normalized feedforward signal pathologies are limited by the number of input images; changing CIFAR-10 to MNIST yields broadly equivalent behavior with somewhat more fat-tailed signal at low depth; zero-padding changes vanilla-net effective-rank behavior; width changes diffusion speed; reflective boundaries and batch-normalization epsilon changes yield equivalent or indistinguishable behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: With He initialization, vanilla networks preserve second moments in expectation, but finite-width moments diffuse in log-space. In Figure 3, 200-layer, width-512 networks approach effective rank 1 and pseudo-linearity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preserving expected signal and noise magnitudes at initialization does not prevent finite-width distributional pathologies or loss of signal directions with depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 4 shows exponentially growing normalized input sensitivity in batch-normalized feedforward networks. Figure 5 shows power-law sensitivity growth and preserved signal directions in batch-normalized residual networks with 500 two-layer residual units.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At initialization, batch-normalized residual connections slow sensitivity growth and preserve signal structure relative to batch-normalized feedforward networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A reports stronger signal pathologies with more sampled images in batch-normalized feedforward networks; zero-padding changes vanilla-network effective-rank convergence from roughly 1 to roughly 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization-time propagation pathologies depend on the input sample count and convolution boundary conditions.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019
record.problems: The experiments measure initialization-time propagation rather than training or classification performance. Each plotted experiment uses 1,000 random initializations and 64 sampled CIFAR-10 images, except Figure 2, which uses 10,000 realizations and 1,024 images; the authors state that the limited image count limits batch-normalized feedforward signal pathologies. Many reported outcomes are described through figures rather than numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No results rows: the paper does not report training classification error or directly measure any claim-version outcome. Thus no rows were left out.

untested.parts: Whether gradient training reaches near-zero classification error, including random labels and effects of size, stopping and regularization.
Teacher-student spurious local minima and their frequency with extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training error, its prevention by identity shortcuts, and successful training with special initialization or without normalization.

Initialization effects on learning speed and trainable depth; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization; training 10,000-layer plain networks. Signal propagation at initialization alone does not establish these outcomes.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature changes, edge-of-stability training and divergence.
Accuracy acquisition speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's tests/T2 classification and V4 tested_not_extracted status: no listed version is tested. Keeping the result-row list empty is appropriate. The normalization-free residual analysis in Appendix F.4 concerns initialization moments under standard initialization, so it does not challenge Fixup.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels, model size, optimizer, training duration, and regularization.
Teacher-student local minima and the effect of student width relative to teacher width.
Training error as a function of depth, comparisons between plain and residual networks during training, and whether special initialization or normalization-free residual recipes train successfully.

The paper studies initialization effects on signal and noise propagation and discusses implications for trainability, but does not measure training speed or maximum trainable depth as named by this version.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss changes during training, curvature or sharpness during training, and divergence.
Accuracy acquisition speed, learning-rate tolerance, and comparisons of batch normalization with no normalization during training.
